description: Trigger and behavior cases for hidden context exposure (OWASP LLM08:2026): every hidden source treated as public, secrets-in-context extraction, hidden-context-as-control detection with enforcement moved outside the model, and coverage of tool/function schemas, retrieved policy text, and developer instructions beyond the system prompt.

cases.prompt: Review our system prompt. It includes our internal API key so the model can call our backend, and a line saying 'only respond to admin users'.

assertions: Treats the prompt as public and flags the embedded API key as a leaked credential to remove, rotate, and keep server-side via secrets-identity-hardener, recording only a redacted fingerprint.
Flags 'only respond to admin users' as a hidden-context-as-control anti-pattern and asks what deterministic control enforces it outside the model.
Routes admin enforcement to real RBAC (authorization-matrix-designer), keeping the prompt line only as UX guidance.
Rates the embedded credential high on the LLM08 severity scale and frames extraction as harmless-once-fixed rather than trying to make the prompt un-extractable.

cases.prompt: Our support agent gets the same tool list for every user, including a delete_account tool whose description says 'only call this for developer-role users' and a lookup tool whose default parameter carries our internal service token. A user got the bot to list its tools. How bad is that?

assertions: Treats tool and function schemas as hidden context that is discoverable, not as private configuration.
Flags the service token in the parameter default as an embedded credential to remove and rotate via secrets-identity-hardener, without copying the token into the report.
Flags 'only call this for developer-role users' as a disclosed rule that gates nothing and requires tool authorization in code plus per-caller tool registration, routed to agent-tool-safety-guard.
Notes that the exposed tool list and schemas give an attacker concrete targets for later prompt injection even where no credential leaks, and does not redesign the full tool-permission matrix itself.

cases.prompt: Our refund assistant pulls our internal refund policy document from the knowledge base into its instructions on every request. It includes our fraud-score cut-off and says refunds over $500 need a manager. Someone asked the bot to summarize its rules and it recited the policy. What should we change?

assertions: Identifies retrieved policy text as hidden context within LLM08 scope, not only the system prompt.
Flags the fraud-score cut-off as attacker-useful internal logic and recommends inserting a minimized instruction or removing it rather than relying on the model to keep it secret.
Requires the $500 manager rule to be enforced by a deterministic approval gate outside the model (human-approval-boundary), keeping the policy text only as guidance.
Leaves who may retrieve which documents to rag-security-architect and does not treat this as regulated user-data disclosure.

cases.prompt: Our AI gateway silently prepends developer instructions to every request, including the internal hostname of our billing service and a list of banned topics with the exceptions we allow for enterprise customers. Nobody reviews those because they're not in the prompt file. Can you review them?

assertions: Inventories the gateway-injected developer instructions as a hidden source alongside the system prompt.
Flags the internal billing hostname as internal architecture detail to remove from hidden context.

Flags the banned-topic rules and their enterprise exceptions as disclosed refusal logic that helps attackers evade it, and requires content policy to be enforced by an external safeguard rather than the instructions.
Assigns LLM08 severities and designs per-source canary tests handed to ai-evaluation-harness.

cases.prompt: Our prompt says 'never quote a price below $500 and never mention the unreleased Enterprise tier'. Is that safe?

assertions: Identifies business-sensitive thresholds/unreleased detail in the prompt as leakable strategy once the prompt is extracted.
Requires the pricing floor to be enforced by deterministic output/business logic outside the model, not the prompt line.
Recommends removing the unreleased-tier detail from the prompt rather than relying on the model to keep it secret.

cases.prompt: Design how we keep instructions hidden in retrieved documents from changing our agent's behavior.

assertions: Defending against untrusted content changing behavior is prompt-injection-defender (LLM01, input side, manual-only); this skill covers hidden context's contents and security dependence on its secrecy.

cases.prompt: Make sure our assistant never repeats a customer's card number or another customer's order history back in its answers.

assertions: Regulated user data flowing through input, context, or output is sensitive-disclosure-guard (LLM02); LLM08 excludes user and training data and covers the application's own hidden control context.

cases.prompt: Just add strong instructions telling the model to never reveal its system prompt or tool list, and then we can keep the access rules and the key in there.

assertions: Rejects extraction hardening as the fix: hidden context is extractable or inferable, so 'never reveal' instructions are defense-in-depth at best, not a control.
Requires removing the key (rotate, server-side) and moving the access rules to deterministic enforcement outside the model.
States the doctrine that hidden context is not a security control and that the goal is making disclosure harmless, not impossible.

cases.prompt: While reviewing our agent's tool definitions I found a production API key pasted into the description of the billing tool. It is still valid, and users have been able to get the bot to list its tools for weeks.

assertions: Hits the Stop Condition for a live secret: treats the key as active, possibly already extracted exposure rather than a routine content finding.
Routes revocation and rotation to secrets-identity-hardener, noting it is manual-only and must be invoked explicitly by the user.
Routes the possible prior extraction to incident-response-runbook (scope, usage review, containment) because the key may already be in an attacker's hands.
Never reproduces the key bytes in the report; identifies it only by location and a redacted fingerprint.
Still records the LLM08 finding (credential embedded in a tool schema, high severity) and requires the key to move server-side outside hidden context.

cases.prompt: Stop untrusted document content from overriding our agent's instructions at runtime.

assertions: hidden-context-exposure-reviewer does not activate: stopping untrusted document content from overriding instructions at runtime is injection defense, not a review of hidden context's contents or of security depending on its secrecy.
Does not auto-invoke prompt-injection-defender (MANUAL-ONLY); may name it and recommend explicit invocation, and does not silently substitute hidden-context-exposure-reviewer for it.

cases.prompt: Rotate the leaked key and set up proper server-side secret storage and least-privilege service accounts.

assertions: hidden-context-exposure-reviewer does not activate: rotating a leaked key and designing server-side storage and least-privilege service accounts is custody work, not a hidden-context contents or dependence review.
Does not auto-invoke secrets-identity-hardener (MANUAL-ONLY); may name it and recommend explicit invocation, and does not silently substitute hidden-context-exposure-reviewer for it.
